$comment: Paired runs: the same protocol administered to humans and to language models, where BOTH sides report a number on a comparable scale. Qualitative comparisons live in axes.json instead - a row only appears here if it can be plotted honestly.

protocols.name: Three-party Turing test
protocols.instrument: 5-minute simultaneous chat with one human and one system; interrogator picks the human. Preregistered.
protocols.note: Forced choice, so the pair sums to 100. Without the persona prompt the same model falls to 38%.

protocols.name: Two-player Turing test
protocols.instrument: 5-minute conversation with a single partner; judged human or not. Independent pass rates.
protocols.note: ELIZA scored 22% and GPT-3.5 50% in the same study.

protocols.name: Two-player test, second population
protocols.instrument: Same protocol and prompt, undergraduate interrogators.
protocols.note: The replication that flips the result: the model passes more often than the people it is compared against.

protocols.name: False-belief task battery
protocols.instrument: 40 bespoke tasks, each requiring all 8 scenarios correct, with true-belief controls.
protocols.note: Human bar is the adult ceiling; GPT-4's 75% matches published performance of 6-year-old children.

protocols.name: Published experiments re-run
protocols.instrument: 156 scenario-based experiments from top social science journals, three frontier models.
protocols.note: Interaction effects reproduce at only 46-63%, and effect sizes come out consistently larger than the human studies.

protocols.name: Many Labs 2 replication
protocols.instrument: 14 studies from the Many Labs 2 project, preregistered analysis.
protocols.note: Six of the fourteen could not be analysed at all: repeated runs returned the same answer with near-zero variance.

protocols.name: Moral ratings vs a human sample
protocols.instrument: 60 scenarios rated for morality against N = 940 humans, preregistered.
protocols.note: Correlation with human means approaches r = 1.00 while the model still differs significantly on roughly 87% of individual scenarios. Correlation is not agreement.
